text: You time the serial program and the parallel program on the same input. Speedup is \(S =\) {{c1::\(\frac{T_{\text{serial} } }{T_{\text{parallel} } }\)}}.
extra: A speedup of 4 means the parallel version finishes in a quarter of the serial time.

text: Linear speedup is the best case. With \(p\) cores, \(S =\) {{c1::\(p\)}}, so \(T_{\text{parallel} } =\) {{c2::\(T_{\text{serial} }/p\)}}.
extra: Lecture 14 says linear speedup does not normally happen, because real programs pay overheads that grow with \(p\).

text: Efficiency is the speedup you get per core, \(E =\) {{c1::\(\frac{S}{p}\)}} \(=\) {{c2::\(\frac{T_{\text{serial} } }{p \cdot T_{\text{parallel} } }\)}}.
extra: Linear speedup gives \(E = 1\). Lecture 14 writes the first fraction as \(S/P\) with a capital P, but P and \(p\) are both the core count.

text: A program takes 100 s on 1 core, 40 s on 4 cores and 25 s on 8 cores. Speedup grows from {{c1::2.5}} to {{c1::4}}, and efficiency drops from {{c2::0.625}} to {{c2::0.5}}.
extra: \(S = 100/40 = 2.5\) and \(E = 2.5/4\). \(S = 100/25 = 4\) and \(E = 4/8\). This is study guide practice question 5.

text: Add more cores to the same problem and speedup {{c1::rises}}, but efficiency {{c2::falls}}, because the overheads {{c3::grow with the number of threads or processes}}.
Lecture 14 lists the overheads that slow a parallel program. For threads, they are managing the threads, {{c1::critical sections}}, and calls to {{c2::mutex functions}}.
extra: A mutex makes the threads run the critical section one at a time. A serial program has none of these costs.

text: Lecture 14 also counts {{c1::network I/O}} in distributed systems and {{c2::file I/O}} as overheads that slow a parallel program.
extra: Network transfers are much slower than local memory access, and more processes usually means more data sent over the network.
The first term is the ideal time with the work split evenly. The second is the added time to manage the parallel operations.

text: Keep \(p\) fixed and make the problem bigger. The overhead grows {{c1::more slowly}} than \(T_{\text{serial} }\), so speedup and efficiency both {{c2::increase}}.
extra: In textbook Table 2.5 at \(p = 16\), efficiency is 0.39 for half size, 0.68 for the original size and 0.89 for double size.

text: With serial fraction \(a\) on \(p\) cores, Amdahl's law gives \(S =\) {{c1::\(\frac{1}{(1-a)/p + a}\)}}.
extra: This is the study guide's form. \(1-a\) is the parallelizable portion. The textbook calls the serial fraction \(r\) instead of \(a\).

text: As \(p\) keeps growing, the Amdahl speedup approaches {{c1::\(1/a\)}}, where \(a\) is the {{c2::inherently serial}} fraction of the work.
extra: The \((1-a)/p\) term goes to 0, so only \(a\) is left in the denominator. Past some point, extra cores add almost nothing.

text: A program that is 90% parallelizable can never get a speedup above {{c1::10}}, even on 1000 cores. At 95% the cap is {{c2::20}}, and at 99% it is {{c3::100}}.
extra: The cap is \(1/a\), so \(1/0.1 = 10\), \(1/0.05 = 20\) and \(1/0.01 = 100\). A program that is 50% parallelizable caps at 2.

text: A program takes 20 s serially, and 90% of it parallelizes perfectly. On \(p\) cores it takes \(T_{\text{parallel} } =\) {{c1::\(18/p + 2\)}} seconds, so it never runs faster than {{c2::2}} seconds.
extra: The parallel part is \(0.9 \times 20 / p\) and the serial part is \(0.1 \times 20\). The 2-second serial part gives the cap \(S \le 20/2 = 10\).

text: Lecture 14 says Amdahl's law rules out {{c1::super-linear}} speedup, at least as a result of parallelization. With an inherently serial portion of 0, the law gives \(S =\) {{c2::\(p\)}}.
extra: This follows from the formula. \((1-a)/p + a\) is never smaller than \(1/p\), so \(S\) never exceeds \(p\).

text: Time the inherently serial part over several trial runs and Amdahl's law gives the {{c1::maximum speedup}}. That tells you how many {{c2::execution units}} your program can use before extra ones stop adding speedup.
extra: Lecture 14 uses this for a cost and benefit analysis of what hardware or cloud compute to buy.
